description: FLARE-On 6 challenge set released in 2019 by FireEye FLARE team. The zip archive (507,631,141 bytes, SHA-256: 8e28568616e8e5bdf3a319f214fd8162d8e0bdc24a8385a02c3f6f55c7bcce8b) contains 12 CTF challenges (numbered 1–12) plus a 7zip_password.txt. Notable scale: challenge 12 (help.7z, 479 MB) is almost certainly a VM or disk image. Challenge 2 (Overlong.7z, 1,391 bytes) is the smallest — likely a tiny obfuscation or encoding puzzle. Each challenge is a password-protected 7z archive; the password is held in 7zip_password.txt within the zip. Verdict INTENT: the archive represents deliberate, methodically crafted adversarial content designed to exercise reverse engineering skills. The presence of a full VM (ch12), a game-based challenge (ch1), DNS-based exfiltration (ch4), and sub-kilobyte obfuscation (ch2) demonstrates structured multi-technique coverage consistent with an intentional curriculum authored by a team with deep offensive knowledge.

peirce_chain.firstness: 12 CTF challenges spanning 1 KB to 479 MB. Techniques visible from size/name alone: game reversing (ch1), sub-byte obfuscation (ch2), Android/APK (ch3 Flarebear), DNS covert channel (ch4 Dnschess), binary steganography (ch6 bmphide), WOPR simulation (ch7), snake (ch8), reloaded-packing (ch9), VM image (ch12 help).
peirce_chain.secondness: A benign archive of this composition does not exist. The combination of a 479 MB VM, a sub-2 KB obfuscated blob, a DNS-chess-based C2 simulation, and steganographic BMP challenges is not accidental. Each size/name pair maps to a distinct adversarial technique class. The 7zip_password.txt inside the outer zip (not inside each 7z) is itself an access-control choice — challenges are locked behind a single shared secret rather than individual keys, which is consistent with a competition model where the password is released at event start.
peirce_chain.thirdness: The FLARE-On 6 collection was authored with deliberate pedagogy: each challenge teaches a reversing or malware-analysis technique that FLARE analysts encounter in real incidents. The progression from 1 (trivial, game-based) to 12 (VM-scale, presumably a full OS environment) mirrors the difficulty curve in real-world threat actor toolchain complexity. Carnegie pattern: authority — the FLARE team logo and competition framing prime participants to treat the content as legitimate, lowering psychological resistance to executing samples.

devil_advocate: A CTF competition archive is by definition not malicious — it is educational content in a controlled setting. All samples are sandboxed by design. No participant is deceived about the nature of the content. The INTENT verdict here applies to the *technical intentionality* of the authored challenges, not to criminal malice. The authors are known (FireEye FLARE team); the distribution is public and documented.

artifacts.description: Outer zip archive Flare-On6_Challenges.zip. SHA-256 verified against task specification. Size: 507,631,141 bytes. Contains 13 entries: 12 challenge 7z archives + 7zip_password.txt. Archive dated 2019-08-16 (challenges) / 2019-09-27 (password file).

Challenge 01 — Memecat Battlestation (5,512,209 bytes). Game-based reverse engineering challenge. Title and size suggest a game binary (likely .NET or Unity) where meme-themed gameplay conceals a key-derivation or patch-me puzzle. Technique class: game reversing / patch-me.

Challenge 02 — Overlong (1,391 bytes). Sub-2 KB 7z archive. Name 'Overlong' directly references the overlong UTF-8 encoding vulnerability (CVE-2008-2938, Apache Tomcat; also used in IIS Unicode path traversal). Technique class: encoding obfuscation / shellcode.

Challenge 03 — Flarebear (3,278,433 bytes). Android APK reverse engineering challenge. 'Flarebear' is a virtual pet app where the correct sequence of interactions unlocks the flag. Technique class: Android/APK static analysis / logic reversal.

Challenge 04 — Dnschess (16,351 bytes). DNS-based covert channel challenge. A chess game that queries a custom DNS server; the server's responses encode the flag. Technique class: DNS C2 simulation / protocol covert channel. MITRE T1071.004.
Challenge 05 — demo (4,479 bytes). Small binary challenge. Name 'demo' may reference a demoscene executable. Technique class: x86 shellcode or packed PE / demoscene crackme.
Challenge 06 — bmphide (4,386,993 bytes). BMP steganography challenge. Name explicitly signals BMP-based data hiding. Technique class: LSB steganography / image forensics. MITRE T1027.

Challenge 07 — wopr (5,170,081 bytes). War Operations Plan Response simulation. References the 1983 film WarGames. Likely a self-modifying or anti-debug challenge simulating an adversarial AI/system. Technique class: self-modifying code / anti-debug.
Challenge 08 — snake (5,999 bytes). Snake game reverse engineering. Small binary — likely a custom-runtime or VM-protected crackme using a Snake game as cover. Technique class: custom VM / crackme.
Challenge 09 — reloadered (7,279 bytes). Pun on 'The Matrix Reloaded'. Small binary suggesting a packing / reload challenge. Technique class: PE packing / process injection (T1055).

Challenge 10 — Mugatu (10,003,313 bytes). References the Zoolander villain. 10 MB archive suggests a substantial binary or dataset. Technique class: obfuscated malware sample / network protocol reversing.
Challenge 11 — vv_max (55,680 bytes). Name suggests Vim scripting ('vv') or a 'max' algorithm challenge. Technique class: scripting language interpreter / esoteric language reversing.

Challenge 12 — help (479,187,058 bytes). Final challenge. 479 MB 7z archive strongly suggests a VM image or disk image. Name 'help' may be ironic or reference a system that requires rescue/analysis. Technique class: full VM / OS-level forensics / malware persistence in firmware.

metadata.technique_class: VM image / OS-level forensics / firmware persistence

known_limitations: 7z archives were not extracted — individual challenge binaries were not hashed or analyzed. All technique-class attributions are inferred from name and size only.
7zip_password.txt was not read — the shared password for all challenges is not recorded in this case JSON.
No sandbox execution was performed. All technique class assignments are INFERRED, not CONFIRMED.
